https://www.dw.com/en/france-protesters-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OLrM Hundreds of arrests have been made as unrest broke out during a day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS Advertisement There have been clashes between police and protesters amid mass rallies across France on Saturday, over high prices and social inequalities and the state of the education system. Police arrest hundreds nationwide The Interior Ministry said that round 550,000 people turned out for the demonstrations, with some 400 arrests made following violent incidents in Paris, Marseilles, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers and elsewhere. "Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," the ministry saidand blamed the unrest on what it described ​as the "hard-left." France protests escalate as unrest spreads across cities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In Paris and Marseille, police fired tear gas at protesters as violent clashes took place. AFP reported that dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux and Lille, where an Apple store was stripped. The windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were also broken by protesters, and AFP journalists reported seeing several parked cars torched. French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in a post on X and warned: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." Buildings set alight amid unrest In Lyon, situated in central France, the city's tourism office was set alight with flames and black smoke seen billowing from the building. Lyon's tourism office was set alight during chaotic scenes Image: Jeff Pachoud/AFP In the city of Limoges, the town hall was also set alight as unrest broke out. The blaze spread from a wing of the building and eventually reached the roof where it continued burning as crowds stood watching. Firefighters were then seen attmepting to douse the flames. The 19th century town hall building was set alight as unrest erupted in Limoges Image: Elise Cabane/MAXPPP/picture alliance Meanwhile in Lille, protesters smashed their way into the town hall of France's northern city of Lille and vandalised the premises before leaving, according to an AFP photographer. Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left. The protests come on the heels of an initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country , with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities. Macron had called "for calm and respect" ahead of the protests, saying that the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property." France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What do we know about the protests in France? More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to protest organizers. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television that "a pretty big turnout" was expected, while a police source told the French AFP news agency that authorities estimate nearly 200,000 people will attend. 40,000 people were expected in the capital, Paris, a police source said Image: Yann Tessier/REUTERS However, the Paris demonstrators faced restrictions, with police banning rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysee avenue, along with other key locations. A march through the center of the city has also been banned. French police are out in force near the Place de la Republique in Paris Image: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS The main Paris demonstration began at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) at the Place de la Republique.. Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas. Protesters clash with riot police officers in Paris Image: Kiran Ridley/AFP Who is taking part in the protests? Students have been joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general. The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melanchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday. The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/21/russ.text: Russia is willing to return to three-way negotiations with the United States and Ukraine on ending the war, the Kremlin said on Wednesday after Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg. However, it complained that recent Ukrainian and European proposals lacked "substance".The talks, which lasted more than three hours in Putin's home city, coincided with the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher jailed in Russia for allegedly fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Witkoff announced the release during the meeting.The Kremlin also said preparations were under way for a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen next month between Putin, US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping, describing it as "the first such meeting in history."Witkoff, who has made several unsuccessful trips to Russia in pursuit of a settlement, arrived in Saint Petersburg a day after what he called a "productive" meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway. He told Putin he saw "some degree of momentum" in the US-led talks.Diesel deal angers Kyiv and EuropeWitkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a recent diesel deal, under which US sanctions on Moscow were eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.The arrangement has provoked outrage in Ukraine and across Europe. It is widely seen as an attempt to bring down fuel prices for American consumers ahead of next month's midterm elections, which are expected to be difficult for Trump's Republican Party.The deal is one of several steps by the Trump administration seen as favourable to Moscow, at a time of growing tension between Washington and Kyiv.Witkoff said the US was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia once the war ends. "We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.Hubbard freed without prisoner swapHubbard was first imprisoned by Russia in 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus. He was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed-door trial in 2024.Russian prosecutors accused him of joining the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and fighting alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later.The Biden administration had classified Hubbard as wrongfully detained.He is the second American released by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of former US Marine Robert Gilman, who had been seriously ill and was jailed on contested charges of assaulting a police officer.His release coincided with Witkoff's visit and came as Trump has taken several steps favourable to Moscow, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv.In an open letter to Trump published by Hostage Aid Worldwide in August, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, praised the president but also claimed her brother had endured "constant beatings, torture and starvation" while in detention.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/09/nvid.text: US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company's board of directors announced on Sunday.A report by The New York Times said that the CEO had admitted to the board that he had been "unfaithful" with a business executive who, according to US intelligence, was gathering information for China.Nvidia is one of the global leaders in the development of artificial intelligence. Its chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced chips have also been targeted by US export restrictions to prevent China from getting the latest semiconductor technology.In a letter addressed to Nvidia employees, Huang said that he took "full responsibility" for his actions, while admitting to being unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues. However, he did not mention the name of the person involved or her reported ties to Beijing.“Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” the 63-year-old wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.”China has consistantly rejected the spying allegations, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun telling a regular briefing on Monday that "the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing."'No reason to believe' that national security has been compromisedThe board leading the company, which is one of the most valuable in the world, says it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised, but that a thorough independent investigation would be carried out. The board added that Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."In his letter to employees, Jensen Huang said, “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.”George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told AFP that "it would be premature to conclude that Jensen poses a threat to US national security before the facts are fully established.""Once you become famous, you will naturally become a target," Chen said."The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised."Last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed close ties with Chinese citizen and chip buyer Alice Huang, and that she was directly sharing information with Beijing.Alice Huang is a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that runs data centres across Southeast Asia and has become Nvidia’s largest customer in the region.Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump was asked on Sunday whether he should have acted on the spying information sooner. However, Trump praised Huang, saying, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He’s done an amazing job for our country.”Trump is heading to the Asia-Pacific summit in China's Shenzhen next week and told reporters Huang is invited, saying: "I don't know but I'll certainly take him."

https://www.irishmirror.ie/news/irish-ne.text: A man appeared in court on Tuesday night charged with the bank holiday murder of his partner in north Dublin. A special sitting of Dublin District Court heard that Daniel Simion Toader made no reply when he was charged with the murder of Loredana Morosanu at their home on Melville Terrace, Finglas in the early hours of hours of Monday morning. Detective Sergeant Niall Murray of Finglas Garda Station told Judge Maire Conneely that he arrested Mr Simion Toader, who appeared in court wearing a blue jumper and grey sweatpants, at the station at 6.58pm on Tuesday. The officer also told the court that Romanian national Mr Simion Toader, 47, with an address at Melville Terrace, Finglas , was charged at the station with the murder of Ms Morosanu at 7.56pm. “He made no reply,” the detective sergeant added. It's alleged he murdered her on Monday morning. Bail is not a matter for the district court and Mr Simion Toader, who did not address the court during the brief hearing but did speak briefly to a Romanian interpreter, was remanded in custody. He is due to appear again at Cloverhill District Court via video link next Tuesday at 10am. Mr Simion Toader was not legally represented in court. That is because of the ongoing free legal aid dispute involving criminal defence solicitors around the country. But Judge Conneely heard that the accused had had eight legal consultations while in custody, and one just before he was brought to court. Det Sgt Murray told the court that Mr Simion Toader’s circumstances of him being charged had been explained to him at length. The hearing lasted just two minutes. The body of Ms Morosanu, 48, was found at her apartment at Melville Terrace in Finglas, north Dublin in the early hours of Monday morning. Ms Morosanu, who worked in a pharmacy in Dublin, had only moved into the apartment in the complex in recent weeks.
